item.title: The Girl Living With The Mauerovás Was Actually 32
item.description: During the 2007 investigation into abuse of two brothers in Kuřim, Czech Republic, authorities discovered that “Anna,” supposedly 13, was adult Barbora Škrlová. In 2008, she received five years in prison; the boys’ mother and aunt received nine and ten years.

item.title: They Killed For A Fortune Corpsewood Manor Never Held
item.description: In December 1982, Charles Scudder and Joseph Odom were murdered at their secluded Georgia home. Avery Brock and Tony West had plotted to steal a fortune they believed was hidden there, but found no cash. Both ultimately received life sentences for the killings.

item.title: A Misdelivered Letter Led Police To Peter Kürten
item.description: A survivor’s letter describing Peter Kürten’s attack reached the wrong recipient, who alerted police. Her account helped identify the Düsseldorf killer in 1930. He was convicted of nine murders and seven attempted murders in 1931 and executed that year.

item.title: An Online Dispute Preceded Satomi Mitarai’s Classroom Killing
item.description: In June 2004, 12-year-old Satomi Mitarai was killed at school in Sasebo, Japan, by an 11-year-old classmate. Police linked the attack to a dispute over online messages. A family court ordered the younger girl into a juvenile facility with counseling.

item.title: The DNA Breakthrough That Exposed David Fuller’s Double Life
item.description: DNA linked hospital electrician David Fuller to the 1987 murders of Wendy Knell and Caroline Pierce in Kent. A search then uncovered evidence of abuse in hospital mortuaries. He pleaded guilty to both murders and received a whole-life sentence in 2021.

item.title: A Missing License Plate Led Police To Joel Rifkin
item.description: In June 1993, Joel Rifkin fled New York troopers who spotted his missing license plate. After he crashed, police found Tiffany Bresciani’s body in his truck. He confessed to killing 17 women and was ultimately convicted of nine murders, receiving 203 years in prison.

item.title: Joe Arridy’s Pardon Came 72 Years After His Execution
item.description: Colorado executed Joe Arridy, a 23-year-old man with an intellectual disability, in 1939. In 2011, Governor Bill Ritter granted a posthumous pardon, citing overwhelming evidence of innocence, including false and coerced confessions and another man’s admission of guilt.
